title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 876–879 (Night 208, continuing nights-207), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 208 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. He walks through the city from the landward gate to the sea gate without meeting a soul, and comes out among its orchards, where a gardener hurries him inside his garden before anyone sees him: the people of the city, he says, are all Magians. Hearing his story, the gardener tells him that the lands of Islam are four months away by sea, a year by land, and that a ship sails once a year to the Ebony Islands and on to the Khālidān Islands of King Shahramān. Qamar al-Zamān stays on as the gardener's hand, turning the water channels and weeping verses for his beloved. The story turns to the Lady Budūr: waking to find her husband and the stone gone, she fears the retinue will grow bold if they learn of it, dresses in his clothes, and leads the caravan on as Qamar al-Zamān, until they camp outside the Ebony City of King Armānūs, whose daughter is Ḥayāt al-Nufūs; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and eighth night,
sentences.n: “The eighth after the two hundred”: al-thāmina, “the eighth”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ وَاسْتَرَاحَ دَخَلَ بَابَ الْمَدِينَةِ وَهُوَ لَا يَعْلَمُ أَيْنَ يَتَوَجَّهُ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā faragha min shiʿrihi wa-istarāḥa dakhala bāba al-madīnati wa-huwa lā yaʿlamu ayna yatawajjahu
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when he-finished from his-verse and-rested, entered (the) gate (of) the-city, and-he not knows where he-turns.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān had finished his verses and rested, he went in at the city gate, not knowing which way to turn.
sentences.n: The print has تمر, a misprint for قمر, corrected here: the name is Qamar al-Zamān, “Moon of the Age”. The night takes up the last sentence of the night before, where he had finished his verses and rested by a stream outside the city. dakhala bāba al-madīnati, “he entered the gate of the city”: dakhala takes its object directly, without a preposition. wa-huwa lā yaʿlamu, “while he did not know”, a circumstantial clause opened by wa-. tawajjaha, Form V, “to turn one's face towards, head for”; the shadda of يتوجّه is printed.

sentences.t: فَشَقَّ الْمَدِينَةَ مِنْ أَوَّلِهَا إِلَى آخِرِهَا وَكَانَ قَدْ دَخَلَ مِنْ بَابِ الْبَرِّ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَمْشِي حَتَّى خَرَجَ مِنْ بَابِ الْبَحْرِ فَلَمْ يُقَابِلْهُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-shaqqa al-madīnata min awwalihā ilā ākhirihā wa-kāna qad dakhala min bābi al-barri wa-lam yazal yamshī ḥattā kharaja min bābi al-baḥri fa-lam yuqābilhu aḥadun min ahlihā
sentences.l: And-he-split the-city from its-first to its-last; and-he-had entered by (the) Gate (of) the-Land, and-not he-ceased walking until he-went-out by (the) Gate (of) the-Sea; and-not met-him anyone of its-people.
sentences.i: He crossed the city from one end to the other: he had come in by the Land Gate, and he kept walking until he went out by the Sea Gate, and not one of its people met him.
sentences.n: shaqqa, “to split”, of a road or a city: to cut straight through it. kāna qad dakhala, “he had entered”: kāna with qad and a perfect gives the pluperfect. bāb al-barr and bāb al-baḥr, “the gate of the land” and “the gate of the sea”: the landward and the seaward gates. lam yazal with an imperfect, “he did not cease …, he kept on …”. yuqābilhu, Form III, “to meet, face”, jussive after lam. The hamza of آخرها is printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ مَدِينَةً عَلَى شَاطِئِ الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat madīnatan ʿalā shāṭiʾi al-baḥri
sentences.l: And-it-was a-city upon (the) shore (of) the-sea.
sentences.i: It was a city on the seashore.
sentences.n: madīnatan is accusative as the predicate of kānat. The ئ of شاطئ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ بَعْدَ أَنْ خَرَجَ مِنْ بَابِ الْبَحْرِ مَشَى وَلَمْ يَزَلْ مَاشِيًا حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَى بَسَاتِينِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَأَشْجَارِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahu baʿda an kharaja min bābi al-baḥri mashā wa-lam yazal māshiyan ḥattā waṣala ilā basātīni al-madīnati wa-ashjārihā
sentences.l: Then indeed-he, after that he-went-out by (the) Gate (of) the-Sea, walked, and-not he-ceased walking until he-arrived at (the) gardens (of) the-city and-its-trees.
sentences.i: Then, once he was out of the Sea Gate, he walked on and kept walking until he came to the city's orchards and trees.
sentences.n: thumma innahu, “then he …”, the storyteller's transition. lam yazal māshiyan: here zāla takes a participle, accusative as its predicate, instead of an imperfect; the sense is the same. basātīn, plural of bustān, “garden, orchard”.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ بَيْنَ الْأَشْجَارِ وَمَشَى فَأَتَى إِلَى بُسْتَانٍ فَوَقَفَ عَلَى بَابِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala bayna al-ashjāri wa-mashā fa-atā ilā bustānin fa-waqafa ʿalā bābihi
sentences.l: And-he-entered between the-trees, and-walked, and-came to a-garden, and-stood at its-gate.
sentences.i: He went in among the trees and walked on until he came to a garden, and stood at its gate.
sentences.n: atā ilā, “to come to”: Classical atā takes its object directly; the later language often adds ilā. waqafa ʿalā, “to stand at, stop by”.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ إِلَيْهِ الْخَوْلِيُّ فَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja ilayhi al-khawliyyu fa-sallama ʿalayhi fa-radda ʿalayhi al-salāma
sentences.l: And-came-out to-him the-gardener, and-he-greeted him, and-he-returned to-him the-greeting.
sentences.i: The gardener came out to him; Qamar al-Zamān greeted him, and he returned the greeting.
sentences.n: khawlī, “gardener, keeper of an orchard”, an Egyptian word. The subjects shift without being named, as often in this prose: the stranger greets, sallama ʿalayhi, and the gardener returns the greeting, radda ʿalayhi al-salāma. The shadda of فسلّم is printed.

sentences.t: فَرَحَّبَ بِهِ الْخَوْلِيُّ وَقَالَ لَهُ الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ الَّذِي أَتَيْتَ سَالِمًا مِنْ أَهْلِ هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-raḥḥaba bihi al-khawliyyu wa-qāla lahu al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī atayta sāliman min ahli hādhihi al-madīnati
sentences.l: And-welcomed him the-gardener, and-said to-him: The-praise (be) to-God, that you-came safe from (the) people (of) this city.
sentences.i: The gardener made him welcome and said to him, “Praise be to God that you have come through safe from the people of this city!
sentences.n: raḥḥaba bi-, Form II, “to bid welcome to”: the verb takes its object with bi-; the shadda of فرحّب is printed. al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī atayta, literally “praise be to God who … you came”: the relative clause has no pronoun returning to God, so alladhī here does the work of “that”, a loose Middle Arabic turn; Classical would say alladhī sallamaka, “who kept you safe”, or al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā an atayta. sālim min, “safe from, unharmed by”.

sentences.t: فَادْخُلْ إِلَى هٰذَا الْبُسْتَانِ سَرِيعًا قَبْلَ أَنْ يَرَاكَ أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-udkhul ilā hādhā al-bustāni sarīʿan qabla an yarāka aḥadun min ahlihā
sentences.l: So-enter into this garden quickly, before that sees-you anyone of its-people.
sentences.i: Come into this garden quickly, before anyone from the city sees you.”
sentences.n: The damma of فادخُل is printed: it marks the imperative udkhul, whose helping vowel u falls away after fa-. qabla an with the subjunctive, “before”: yarāka, “he sees you”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ دَخَلَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ إِلَى ذٰلِكَ الْبُسْتَانِ وَهُوَ ذَاهِلُ الْعَقْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika dakhala Qamaru al-Zamāni ilā dhālika al-bustāni wa-huwa dhāhilu al-ʿaqli
sentences.l: And-at that, entered Qamar al-Zamān into that garden, and-he (was) bewildered (of) the-mind.
sentences.i: At that Qamar al-Zamān went into the garden, his wits all astray.
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda dhālika, “and thereupon”, a stock link in the narrative. dhāhil al-ʿaqli, “distracted of mind”: an active participle with a defining genitive, “dazed in his wits”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِلْخَوْلِيِّ مَا حِكَايَةُ أَهْلِ هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَمَاخَبَرُهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla li-al-khawliyyi mā ḥikāyatu ahli hādhihi al-madīnati wa-mā khabaruhum
sentences.l: And-he-said to-the-gardener: What (is the) story (of the) people (of) this city, and-what (is) their-news?
sentences.i: And he said to the gardener, “What is the story of the people of this city? What is their case?”
sentences.n: li-al-khawliyyi, “to the gardener”: li- marks the one spoken to. The print sets wa-mā khabaruhum, “and what is their news”, as one word, وماخبرهم; it is kept as set.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ أَهْلَ هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ كُلَّهُمْ مَجُوسٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu iʿlam anna ahla hādhihi al-madīnati kullahum majūsun
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Know that (the) people (of) this city, all-of-them, (are) Magians.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Know that the people of this city are all of them Magians.
sentences.n: iʿlam anna, “know that”, the usual way a speaker opens a piece of information. kullahum, “all of them”, stands in apposition to ahla and so shares its accusative after anna. majūs, “Magians”, the old Arabic name for Zoroastrians; in the Nights it is the stock word for any fire-worshipping unbeliever.

sentences.t: فَبِاللّٰهِ عَلَيْكَ أَخْبِرْنِي كَيْفَ أَتَيْتَ إِلَى هٰذَا الْمَكَانِ وَمَا سَبَبُ مَجِيئِكَ إِلَى بِلَادِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-bi-Allāhi ʿalayka akhbirnī kayfa atayta ilā hādhā al-makāni wa-mā sababu majīʾika ilā bilādinā
sentences.l: So-by-God upon-you, tell-me how you-came to this place, and-what (is the) cause (of) your-coming to our-lands.
sentences.i: But by God I beg you, tell me how you came to this place, and what has brought you to our country.”
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God (I lay it) upon you”, the formula of earnest entreaty: bi- is the particle of oath. akhbirnī, Form IV imperative, “inform me”. The ئ of مجيئك is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ الْخَوْلِيَّ بِجَمِيعِ مَا جَرَى لَهُ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbara Qamaru al-Zamāni al-khawliyya bi-jamīʿi mā jarā lahu min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi
sentences.l: And-informed Qamar al-Zamān the-gardener of-all what happened to-him, from its-first to its-last.
sentences.i: So Qamar al-Zamān told the gardener everything that had happened to him, from first to last.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-, “to inform someone of”: the verb takes the person directly and the matter with bi-. jarā li-, “to happen to”. The hamza of آخره is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْخَوْلِيُّ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ يَا وَلَدِي أَنَّ بِلَادَ الْإِسْلَامِ بَعِيدَةٌ مِنْ هُنَا وَبَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَنَا أَرْبَعَةُ أَشْهُرٍ فِى الْبَحْرِ وَأَمَّا فِى الْبَرِّ فَسَنَةٌ كَامِلَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-khawliyyu ghāyata al-ʿajabi wa-qāla lahu iʿlam yā waladī anna bilāda al-islāmi baʿīdatun min hunā wa-baynahā wa-baynanā arbaʿatu ashhurin fī al-baḥri wa-ammā fī al-barri fa-sanatun kāmilatun
sentences.l: And-wondered the-gardener (the) utmost (of) the-wonder, and-said to-him: Know, O my-son, that (the) lands (of) Islam (are) far from here, and-between-them and-between-us (are) four months on the-sea; and-as-for on the-land, then-a-year complete.
sentences.i: The gardener was utterly astonished, and said to him, “Know, my son, that the lands of Islam are far from here: between them and us lie four months by sea, and by land a full year.
sentences.n: ghāyata al-ʿajabi, “to the utmost of wonder”, an accusative standing for the verbal noun. baynahā wa-baynanā, “between them and us”: Arabic repeats bayna with each pronoun. arbaʿatu ashhurin: arbaʿa takes the feminine-looking form before the masculine shahr, “month”. ammā … fa-, “as for …, then …”: the fa- opens the answer to ammā. The print spells fī both فى and في.

sentences.t: وَأَنَّ عِنْدَنَا مَرْكَبًا تُقْلِعُ وَتُسَافِرُ كُلَّ سَنَةٍ بِبَضَائِعَ إِلَى أَوَّلِ بِلَادِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَتَسِيرُ مِنْ هُنَا إِلَى بَحْرِ جَزَائِرِ الْآبَنُوسِ وَمِنْهَا إِلَى جَزَائِرِ خَالِدَانَ الَّتِي مَلِكُهَا الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ
sentences.tr: wa-anna ʿindanā markaban tuqliʿu wa-tusāfiru kulla sanatin bi-baḍāʾiʿa ilā awwali bilādi al-islāmi wa-tasīru min hunā ilā baḥri jazāʾiri al-ābanūsi wa-minhā ilā jazāʾiri Khālidāna allatī malikuhā al-maliku Shahramānu
sentences.l: And-that with-us (is) a-ship (that) sets-sail and-travels every year with-goods to (the) first (of the) lands (of) Islam, and-goes from here to (the) sea (of the) Islands (of) the-Ebony, and-from-there to (the) Islands (of) Khālidān, whose king (is) King Shahramān.
sentences.i: But we have a ship that sets sail every year with merchandise for the nearest of the lands of Islam. It goes from here to the sea of the Ebony Islands, and from there to the Khālidān Islands, whose king is King Shahramān.”
sentences.n: wa-anna, “and that”, still hangs on iʿlam, “know”. markab, “ship”, is a masculine noun, but the verbs that describe it, tuqliʿu, tusāfiru, tasīru, are feminine: the speaker thinks of it as safīna, the ordinary feminine word for a ship, a common slip of agreement in this prose. aqlaʿa, Form IV, “to set sail”, literally “to raise the sail”. bi-baḍāʾiʿa, “with goods”: bi- is “carrying”; baḍāʾiʿ, plural of biḍāʿa, is diptote. awwal bilād al-islām, “the first of the lands of Islam”, the nearest Muslim country. Khālidān is the island kingdom of Qamar al-Zamān's father, King Shahramān, where the tale began; the name is taken as diptote. The ئ of جزائر and the آ of الآبنوس are printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ تَفَكَّرَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فِي نَفْسِهِ سَاعَةً وَعَلِمَ أَنَّهُ لَا أَوْفَقَ لَهُ مِنْ قُعُودِهِ فِى الْبُسْتَانِ عِنْدَ الْخَوْلِيِّ وَيَعْمَلُ عِنْدَهُ مُرَابِعًا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika tafakkara Qamaru al-Zamāni fī nafsihi sāʿatan wa-ʿalima annahu lā awfaqa lahu min quʿūdihi fī al-bustāni ʿinda al-khawliyyi wa-yaʿmalu ʿindahu murābiʿan
sentences.l: And-at that, pondered Qamar al-Zamān in himself an-hour, and-knew that-it, no more-fitting (thing) for-him than his-staying in the-garden with the-gardener, and-he-works with-him (as) a-sharecropper.
sentences.i: At that Qamar al-Zamān thought it over to himself for a while, and saw that nothing suited him better than to stay on in the garden with the gardener and work for him as his garden hand.
sentences.n: tafakkara fī nafsihi, “he reflected within himself”. lā awfaqa lahu min, “there is nothing more fitting for him than”: lā denying a whole class takes the accusative without tanwīn, and awfaq is the elative (comparative) from the root w-f-q, “to suit, fit”. wa-yaʿmalu, “and (that) he works”: the imperfect is simply coordinated with the verbal noun quʿūdihi, a loose Middle Arabic join; Classical would want wa-ʿamalihi or wa-an yaʿmala. murābiʿ, here and in al-murābiʿ just below, is a word of the farming country, not of the dictionaries of Classical Arabic. We take it as the partner on the land who works it for a quarter (rubʿ) of the yield, a sharecropper, hence generally a garden hand; the vowels are our reading, and the word may have had a looser sense of hired labourer by this time.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِلْخَوْلِيِّ هَلْ تَقْبَلُنِي عِنْدَكَ لِأَجْلِ الْمُرَابِعِ فِي هٰذَا الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla li-al-khawliyyi hal taqbalunī ʿindaka li-ajli al-murābiʿi fī hādhā al-bustāni
sentences.l: And-he-said to-the-gardener: Will you-accept-me with-you for-the-sake (of) the-sharecropping in this garden?
sentences.i: So he said to the gardener, “Will you take me on to work this garden with you for a share?”
sentences.n: li-al-khawliyyi: li- marks the one spoken to. li-ajli, “for the sake of, for the purpose of”. al-murābiʿ here seems to name the work rather than the worker, “for the sharecropping”: either the word was used loosely so, or the print has dropped the -a of al-murābaʿa, “the sharecropping contract”. We keep the print and read it al-murābiʿ; the reading is doubtful.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Hearing and-obedience!
sentences.i: The gardener answered him, “Hearing and obedience.”
sentences.n: samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “hearing and obedience”: two verbal nouns in the accusative, as if after an unspoken verb, the stock reply of consent.

sentences.t: فَعَلَّمَهُ الْخَوْلِيُّ تَحْوِيلَ الْمَاءِ عَلَى بُيُوتِ الْأَشْجَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿallamahu al-khawliyyu taḥwīla al-māʾi ʿalā buyūti al-ashjāri
sentences.l: And-taught-him the-gardener (the) turning (of) the-water onto (the) houses (of) the-trees.
sentences.i: The gardener taught him how to turn the water into the basins round the trees.
sentences.n: ʿallama, Form II, “to teach”, takes both the pupil and the thing taught as direct objects; the shadda of فعلّمه is printed. taḥwīl al-māʾ, “turning the water”, the work of opening and damming the little channels of an irrigated garden. buyūt al-ashjār, literally “the houses of the trees”: we take these to be the shallow basins banked up round each tree to hold the water, which the gardener's word calls its “house”; the expression is not in the Classical lexica. The hamza of الماء is printed.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يُحَوِّلُ الْمَاءَ وَيَقْطَعُ الْحَشِيشَ بِالْفَأْسِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra Qamaru al-Zamāni yuḥawwilu al-māʾa wa-yaqṭaʿu al-ḥashīsha bi-al-faʾsi
sentences.l: And-began Qamar al-Zamān turns the-water and-cuts the-grass with-the-axe.
sentences.i: So Qamar al-Zamān set to turning the water and cutting the weeds with the hoe.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to …, he went on …”. ḥashīsh, “dry grass, herbage”, here the weeds of the garden. bi-al-faʾsi, “with the axe”: bi- marks the tool. faʾs is properly an axe; in the garden it must be the heavy hoe or mattock used for weeding and for cutting the channels. The print spells it الفاس, and we supply the hamza; Middle Arabic said fās. The shadda of يحوّل is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَلْبَسَهُ الْخَوْلِيُّ بِشْتًا قَصِيرًا أَزْرَقَ إِلَى رُكْبَتَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-albasahu al-khawliyyu bishtan qaṣīran azraqa ilā rukbatayhi
sentences.l: And-clothed-him the-gardener (in) a-cloak short, blue, to his-two-knees.
sentences.i: And the gardener dressed him in a short blue smock that came down to his knees.
sentences.n: albasa, Form IV, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the person and the garment. bisht, a word from Persian, is a coarse woollen outer garment, cloak or smock; the word lives on for a cloak in the Gulf today. Here it is the working dress of a garden hand, short and blue, a far cry from a prince's robes. azraq, “blue”, is diptote, so azraqa has no tanwīn. rukbatayhi, dual, “his two knees”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ عِنْدَهُ يَسْقِي الْأَشْجَارَ وَيَبْكِي بِدُمُوعٍ غِزَارٍ وَلَا يَقِرُّ لَهُ قَرَارٌ بِاللَّيْلِ وَلَا بِالنَّهَارِ مِنْ أَجْلِ غُرْبَتِهِ وَفِي مَحْبُوبَتِهِ يُنْشِدُ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra ʿindahu yasqī al-ashjāra wa-yabkī bi-dumūʿin ghizārin wa-lā yaqirru lahu qarārun bi-al-layli wa-lā bi-al-nahāri min ajli ghurbatihi wa-fī maḥbūbatihi yunshidu al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: And-he-began with-him waters the-trees, and-weeps with-tears abundant, and-not settles for-him a-settling by-the-night nor by-the-day, because-of his-exile; and-on his-beloved he-recites the-verses.
sentences.i: So he lived with the gardener, watering the trees and weeping in floods of tears; he found no rest by night or by day for being far from home, and he recited verses on his beloved.
sentences.n: The sentence runs in rhymed prose: ghizār, nahār, ashʿār. bi-dumūʿin ghizārin, “with abundant tears”: bi- is “with”. lā yaqirru lahu qarārun, literally “no settling settles for him”, an idiom for being unable to find rest; the shadda of يقرّ is not printed. bi-al-layli, bi-al-nahāri: bi- of time, “by night, by day”. ghurba, “being a stranger in a foreign land”. fī maḥbūbatihi, “about his beloved”: fī marks the subject of the verses, and is put first for the rhyme.

sentences.t: فَمِنْ جُمْلَةِ ذٰلِكَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتُ
sentences.tr: fa-min jumlati dhālika hādhihi al-abyātu
sentences.l: And-of (the) whole (of) that (are) these verses:
sentences.i: Among them were these lines:
sentences.n: min jumlati dhālika, “among all that”, the formula that brings on one specimen out of many.

sentences.t:
لَنَا عِنْدَكُمْ وَعْدٌ فَهَلَّا وَفَيْتُمُ * وَقُلْتُمْ لَنَا قَوْلًا فَهَلَّا فَعَلْتُمُ
سَهِرْنَا عَلَى حُكْمِ الْغَرَامِ وَنِمْتُمُ * وَلَيْسَ سَوَاءٌ سَاهِرُونَ وَنُوَّمُ
وَكُنَّا عَهِدْنَا اَنَّنَا نَكْتُمُ الْهَوَى * فَاَغْرَاكُمُ الْوَاشِي وَقَالَ وَقُلْتُمُ
فَيَا اَيُّهَا الْاَحْبَابُ فِى السُّخْطِ وَالرِّضَى * عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ اَنْتُمُ الْقَصْدُ اَنْتُمُ
وَلِي عِنْدَ بَعْضِ النَّاسِ قَلْبٌ مُعَذَّبٌ * فَيَا لَيْتَهُ يَرْثِي لِحَالِي وَيَرْحَمُ
وَمَا كُلُّ عَيْنٍ مِثْلُ عَيْنِي قَرِيحَةٌ * وَلَا كُلُّ قَلْبٍ مِثْلُ قَلْبِي مُتَيَّمُ
ظَلَمْتُمْ وَقُلْتُمْ اِنَّمَا الْحُبُّ ظَالِمٌ * صَدَقْتُمْ كَذَا كَانَ الْحَدِيثُ صَدَقْتُمُ
سَلُوا مُغْرَمًا لَا يَنْقُضُ الدَّهْرَ عَهْدَهُ * وَلَوْ كَانَ فِيْ اَحْشَائِهِ النَّارُ تُضْرَمُ
اِذَا كَانَ خَصْمِي فِى الصَّبَابَةِ حَاكِمِي * لِمَنْ اَشْتَكِي حَالِي لِمَنْ اَتَظَلَّمُ
وَلَوْلَا افْتِقَارِي فِى الْهَوَى وَصَبَابَتِي * لَمَا كَانَ لِي فِى الْعِشْقِ قَلْبٌ مُتَيَّمُ
sentences.tr:
lanā ʿindakum waʿdun fa-hallā wafaytumu * wa-qultum lanā qawlan fa-hallā faʿaltumu
sahirnā ʿalā ḥukmi al-gharāmi wa-nimtumu * wa-laysa sawāʾun sāhirūna wa-nuwwamu
wa-kunnā ʿahidnā annanā naktumu al-hawā * fa-aghrākumu al-wāshī wa-qāla wa-qultumu
fa-yā ayyuhā al-aḥbābu fī al-sukhṭi wa-al-riḍā * ʿalā kulli ḥālin antumu al-qaṣdu antumu
wa-lī ʿinda baʿḍi al-nāsi qalbun muʿadhdhabun * fa-yā laytahu yarthī li-ḥālī wa-yarḥamu
wa-mā kullu ʿaynin mithlu ʿaynī qarīḥatun * wa-lā kullu qalbin mithlu qalbī mutayyamu
ẓalamtum wa-qultum innamā al-ḥubbu ẓālimun * ṣadaqtum kadhā kāna al-ḥadīthu ṣadaqtumu
salū mughraman lā yanquḍu al-dahra ʿahdahu * wa-law kāna fī aḥshāʾihi al-nāru tuḍramu
idhā kāna khaṣmī fī al-ṣabābati ḥākimī * li-man ashtakī ḥālī li-man ataẓallamu
wa-lawlā iftiqārī fī al-hawā wa-ṣabābatī * la-mā kāna lī fī al-ʿishqi qalbun mutayyamu
sentences.l:
To-us with-you (is) a-promise; so-why-not have-you-kept (it)? * And-you-said to-us a-word; so-why-not have-you-done (it)?
We-stayed-awake under (the) rule (of) the-passion, and-you-slept; * and-not (are) equal wakeful-ones and-sleepers.
And-we-had pledged that-we hide the-love; * but-incited-you the-slanderer, and-he-spoke and-you-spoke.
So-O you the-beloved-ones, in the-anger and-the-favour, * upon every state you (are) the-aim, you!
And-to-me with some (of) the-people (is) a-heart tormented; * so-O would-that-he pities my-state and-has-mercy!
And-not every eye, like my-eye, (is) ulcered, * and-not every heart, like my-heart, (is) love-enslaved.
You-wronged, and-you-said: Only the-love (is) a-wrongdoer. * You-spoke-true; thus was the-saying; you-spoke-true!
Ask a-love-smitten-one (who) not breaks the-time his-pledge, * even-if were in his-entrails the-fire being-kindled.
When is my-adversary in the-ardour my-judge, * to-whom (shall) I-complain-of my-state, to-whom (shall) I-plead-my-wrong?
And-were-it-not-for my-need in the-passion and-my-ardour, * not would-be for-me in the-love a-heart love-enslaved.
sentences.i:
You made us a promise: why have you not kept it? * You gave us your word: why have you not done it?
We lay awake at passion's bidding while you slept, * and those who wake and those who sleep are not the same.
We had sworn to one another to keep our love concealed, * but the slanderer egged you on: he talked, and so did you.
O my beloved, in anger and in favour, * come what may, you are my goal, you only.
I have a heart in someone's keeping, a heart in torment: * if only that one would feel for my plight and show mercy!
Not every eye is raw with weeping as mine is, * nor every heart enslaved by love as mine is.
You did wrong, and then you said, “Love is the wrongdoer.” * You spoke the truth; that is how the saying goes; you spoke the truth.
Ask one smitten with love who never breaks his pledge, * though fire were kindled in his entrails.
If my adversary in love is also my judge, * to whom shall I complain of my state, to whom bring my wrong?
Were it not for my need in passion and my longing, * I should have no heart enslaved by love.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is ṭawīl, and every line rhymes in -mu; where the rhyme falls on a pronoun the print writes the long form -tumu (wafaytumu, faʿaltumu, nimtumu), the old pronoun ending that verse keeps. hallā, “why not?”, with a perfect is a reproach for something left undone. nuwwam, “sleepers”, plural of nāʾim. al-wāshī, “the slanderer, the tale-bearer”, the stock villain of love poetry who spreads the lovers' secret. al-qaṣdu, “the aim, the goal”, that towards which one sets out. In the fifth line baʿḍ al-nās, “some of the people”, is a lover's veiled way of naming the beloved, and the -hu of laytahu, “would that he”, returns to that someone. In the sixth line the predicates qarīḥatun, “ulcered”, of an eye sore with weeping, and mutayyamu, “enslaved by love”, are nominative after mā and lā, the usage of the tribe of Tamīm rather than the accusative of the Ḥijāz. al-dahra, “ever”: the accusative of time, “for all time”. tuḍramu, “is kindled”, the passive of aḍrama. taẓallama, Form V, “to complain of a wrong”. lawlā … la-mā kāna, “were it not for … there would not be”: the answer to lawlā takes la-. ṣabāba, “ardent longing”; gharām, hawā and ʿishq are three more names for love. The print sets a bare alif without hamza in اَنَّنَا, فَاَغْرَاكُمُ, اَيُّهَا, الْاَحْبَابُ, اَنْتُمُ, اِنَّمَا, اَحْشَائِهِ, اِذَا, اَشْتَكِي and اَتَظَلَّمُ, spells al-riḍā with ى, and points fī as فِيْ once; all are kept.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ وَمَا جَرَى لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ ابْنِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna wa-mā jarā li-Qamari al-Zamāni ibni al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: This (is) what was and-what happened to-Qamar al-Zamān, son (of) King Shahramān.
sentences.i: So much for what befell Qamar al-Zamān, son of King Shahramān.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna … wa-ammā mā kāna, “this is what happened to … ; but as for …”: the storyteller's formula for leaving one thread of the tale and taking up another. li- here is “to”, marking the one it happened to. ibni is genitive, in apposition to Qamar al-Zamān; Shahramāna is diptote, so its genitive ends in -a.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ زَوْجَتِهِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ فَإِنَّهَا لَمَّا انْتَبَهَتْ مِنْ نَوْمِهَا طَلَبَتْ زَوْجَهَا قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ فَلَمْ تَجِدْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri zawjatihi al-sitti Budūra binti al-maliki al-Ghayūri fa-innahā lammā intabahat min nawmihā ṭalabat zawjahā Qamara al-Zamāni fa-lam tajidhu
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) his-wife, the-Lady Budūr, daughter (of) King al-Ghayūr, then-indeed-she, when she-woke from her-sleep, sought her-husband Qamar al-Zamān, and-not she-found-him.
sentences.i: But as for his wife, the Lady Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr: when she woke from her sleep she looked for her husband Qamar al-Zamān, and could not find him.
sentences.n: The print has تجدة, a misprint for تجده, corrected here: fa-lam tajidhu, “and she did not find him”, the jussive of wajada after lam. al-sitt, “the lady”, a colloquial title of respect for a woman of rank, from sayyida; it stands before her name as al-sayyida would. Budūr, “full moons”, is diptote, so its genitive ends in -a. al-Ghayūr, “the Jealous”, is her father's name. fa-innahā answers ammā: the fa- opens the answer, and inna takes the pronoun.

sentences.t: وَرَأَتْ سِرْوَالَهَا مَحْلُولًا فَافْتَقَدَتِ الْعُقْدَةَ الَّتِي عَلَيْهَا الْفَصُّ فَوَجَدَتْهَا مَحْلُولَةً وَالْفَصَّ مَعْدُومًا
sentences.tr: wa-raʾat sirwālahā maḥlūlan fa-iftaqadati al-ʿuqdata allatī ʿalayhā al-faṣṣu fa-wajadathā maḥlūlatan wa-al-faṣṣa maʿdūman
sentences.l: And-she-saw her-trousers untied, and-she-searched-for the-knot which upon-it (was) the-stone, and-found-it untied, and-the-stone missing.
sentences.i: She saw that her drawers were untied, and she felt for the knot that held the stone, and found it undone and the stone gone.
sentences.n: sirwāl, “trousers, drawers”, the loose trousers held up by a drawstring, on which Budūr had tied the red stone. raʾā and wajada take an object and then a word describing its state: maḥlūlan, “untied”; wa-al-faṣṣa maʿdūman, “and the stone missing”, is a second such pair, both in the accusative. iftaqada, Form VIII, “to look for something one misses”. allatī ʿalayhā al-faṣṣu, “which had the stone on it”: the -hā returns to the knot, as Arabic relative clauses require. maʿdūm, “non-existent”, hence “lost, gone”. The hamza of رأت is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا يَا لَلّٰهِ الْعَجَبُ أَيْنَ زَوْجِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat fī nafsihā yā la-llāhi al-ʿajabu ayna zawjī
sentences.l: And-she-said in herself: O for-God! The-wonder! Where (is) my-husband?
sentences.i: She said to herself, “Good God, how strange! Where is my husband?
sentences.n: yā la-llāhi, “O God!”, the cry of appeal and astonishment, as in the last night: the lām before the one appealed to takes a fatḥa, and the print points it, لَله. Here the print sets yā apart. al-ʿajabu, “the wonder!”, stands on its own, an exclamation, where the full Classical phrase is yā la-llāhi li-al-ʿajabi.

sentences.t: كَأَنَّهُ أَخَذَ الْفَصَّ وَرَاحَ وَهُوَ لَايَعْلَمُ السِّرَّ الَّذِي هُوَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: kaʾannahu akhadha al-faṣṣa wa-rāḥa wa-huwa lā yaʿlamu al-sirra alladhī huwa fīhi
sentences.l: As-if-he took the-stone and-went, and-he not knows the-secret which it (is) in-it.
sentences.i: It seems he took the stone and went off, and yet he does not know the secret that is in it.
sentences.n: kaʾanna, “as if”, here “it seems that”: ka- of likeness fused with anna. rāḥa, “to go away”, in the later language the common verb for going. al-sirr alladhī huwa fīhi, “the secret which is in it”: we take huwa as the secret and fīhi as the stone; it can also be read with huwa the stone and fīhi the secret, “the secret the stone is wrapped in”. Budūr knows the stone holds some hidden virtue; what it is, the tale has not yet said. The print sets lā yaʿlamu as one word, لايعلم; it is kept. The hamza of كأنه is printed.

sentences.t: فَيَاتُرَى أَيْنَ ذَهَبَ
sentences.tr: fa-yā turā ayna dhahaba
sentences.l: And-O, is-it-seen, where he-went?
sentences.i: I wonder, where can he have gone?
sentences.n: yā turā, literally “O, is it seen?”, from the passive of raʾā: a Middle Arabic phrase for “I wonder”, still alive in the spoken language. The print sets fa-yā turā as one word, فياترى; it is kept.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ لَابُدَّلَهُ مِنْ أَمْرٍ عَجِيبٍ اقْتَضَى رَوَاحَهُ وَإِلَّا مَا كَانَ يَقْدِرُ أَنْ يُفَارِقَنِي سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: wa-lākin lā budda lahu min amrin ʿajībin iqtaḍā rawāḥahu wa-illā mā kāna yaqdiru an yufāriqanī sāʿatan
sentences.l: But no escape for-it from a-matter strange (that) required his-going; and-otherwise not he-was able that he-leave-me an-hour.
sentences.i: But there must be some strange matter behind it that made him go; otherwise he could not bear to be parted from me for an hour.
sentences.n: lā budda lahu min, literally “there is no escape for it from”: “it must be due to”. The -hu of lahu is his going off, or the thing itself. The print sets lā budda lahu as one word, لابدله; it is kept. iqtaḍā, Form VIII, “to require, call for”. rawāḥ, “going away”, the verbal noun of rāḥa. wa-illā, “and if not, otherwise”. fāraqa, Form III, “to part from”.

sentences.t: فَلَعَنَ اللّٰهُ الْفَصَّ وَلَعَنَ سَاعَتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-laʿana Allāhu al-faṣṣa wa-laʿana sāʿatahu
sentences.l: So-cursed God the-stone, and-cursed its-hour!
sentences.i: God curse the stone, and curse its hour!”
sentences.n: laʿana Allāhu, “God cursed”: the perfect in a curse, as in a blessing, expresses a wish, “may God curse”. sāʿatahu, “its hour”, the hour of the stone's coming into being or into her life.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ تَفَكَّرَتْ وَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا إِنْ خَرَجْتُ إِلَى الْحَاشِيَةِ وَأَعْلَمْتُهُمْ بِفَقْدِ زَوْجِي يَطْمَعُوا فِيَّ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-sitta Budūra tafakkarat wa-qālat fī nafsihā in kharajtu ilā al-ḥāshiyati wa-aʿlamtuhum bi-faqdi zawjī yaṭmaʿū fiyya
sentences.l: Then indeed the-Lady Budūr pondered, and-said in herself: If I-go-out to the-retinue and-inform-them of-(the)-loss (of) my-husband, they-will-covet me.
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr thought it over, and said to herself, “If I go out to the retinue and tell them that my husband is lost, they will have designs on me.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”: inna puts al-sitta Budūra in the accusative. al-ḥāshiya, “the retinue, attendants”, those about a ruler, literally “the fringe, the border”. aʿlama … bi-, Form IV, “to inform someone of”: bi- marks the matter told. yaṭmaʿū, “they will covet”: the answer to in, “if”, is in the jussive, so the plural has no final -na; this is in fact regular Classical grammar, though the later language drops the -na everywhere. ṭamiʿa fī, “to covet, set one's greed on”: fī marks the object of desire. The shadda of فيّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ لَابُدَّ مِنَ الْحِيلَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin lā budda mina al-ḥīlati
sentences.l: But no escape from the-stratagem.
sentences.i: No, there is nothing for it but a stratagem.”
sentences.n: lā budda min, “there is no escape from, one must have”. The print sets لابدّ as one word and points its shadda; both are kept. ḥīla, “stratagem, ruse”.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتْ وَلَبِسَتْ ثِيَابًا مِنْ ثِيَابِ زَوْجِهَا قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَلَبِسَتْ عِمَامَةً كَعِمَامَتِهِ وَلَبِسَتِ الْخُفَّ وَضَرَبَتْ لَهَا لِثَامًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat wa-labisat thiyāban min thiyābi zawjihā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-labisat ʿimāmatan ka-ʿimāmatihi wa-labisati al-khuffa wa-ḍarabat lahā lithāman
sentences.l: And-she-rose, and-put-on clothes of (the) clothes (of) her-husband Qamar al-Zamān, and-put-on a-turban like-his-turban, and-put-on the-boot, and-struck for-herself a-face-veil.
sentences.i: So she rose and put on some of her husband Qamar al-Zamān's clothes, and a turban like his, and boots, and drew a veil across her face.
sentences.n: ka-ʿimāmatihi, “like his turban”: ka- is “like”. khuff, “boot”, the soft leather riding boot; the singular stands for the pair. ḍarabat lahā lithāman, “she struck a lithām for herself”: ḍaraba is “to put on, set up”, as of a tent or a veil, and lahā, “for herself”, is the later language's reflexive. The lithām is the cloth a man winds over his mouth and the lower face, so with it she can pass for her husband.

sentences.t: وَحَطَّتْ فِي مِحَفَّتِهَا جَارِيَةً وَخَرَجَتْ مِنْ خَيْمَتِهَا وَنَادَتْ عَلَى الْغِلْمَانِ فَقَدَّمُوا لَهَا الْجَوَادَ فَرَكِبَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaṭṭat fī miḥaffatihā jāriyatan wa-kharajat min khaymatihā wa-nādat ʿalā al-ghilmāni fa-qaddamū lahā al-jawāda fa-rakibat
sentences.l: And-she-put in her-litter a-slave-girl, and-went-out from her-tent, and-called upon the-pages, and-they-brought-forward for-her the-steed, and-she-mounted.
sentences.i: She put a slave-girl in her litter in her place, went out of her tent and called for the pages, who brought her the horse, and she mounted.
sentences.n: ḥaṭṭa, “to put, set down”, the everyday Middle Arabic verb for “to put” (Classical waḍaʿa). miḥaffa, “litter”, a covered seat carried on a camel, in which a lady travels; with a slave-girl inside, the caravan will think its mistress is still there. nādā ʿalā, “to call for”: Classical nādā takes its object directly; the later language adds ʿalā. qaddama li-, Form II, “to bring up to”: li- marks the one it is brought for. jawād, “steed, swift horse”.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَتْ بِشَدِّ الْأَحْمَالِ فَشُدَّتْ وَأَمَرَتْ بِالرَّحِيلِ فَسَافَرُوا
sentences.tr: wa-amarat bi-shaddi al-aḥmāli fa-shuddat wa-amarat bi-al-raḥīli fa-sāfarū
sentences.l: And-she-commanded the-binding (of) the-loads, and-they-were-bound; and-she-commanded the-departure, and-they-travelled.
sentences.i: She gave orders for the loads to be bound on, and they were bound, and for the march to begin, and they set out.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes the thing commanded with bi-. shadd, “binding, fastening”, the loading of the baggage onto the beasts; shuddat, “they were bound”, the passive, with the broken plural aḥmāl taking a feminine singular verb. raḥīl, “departure, breaking camp”. The shadda in بشدّ and in فشدّت is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَخْفَتْ أَمْرَهَا فَلَمْ يَشُكَّ أَحَدٌ أَنَّهَا قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ لِأَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تُشْبِهُهُ فِي قَوَامِهِ وَوَجْهِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhfat amrahā fa-lam yashukka aḥadun annahā Qamaru al-Zamāni li-annahā kānat tushbihuhu fī qawāmihi wa-wajhihi
sentences.l: And-she-hid her-affair, and-not doubted anyone that-she (was) Qamar al-Zamān, because-she was resembling-him in his-stature and-his-face.
sentences.i: She kept her secret, and no one doubted that she was Qamar al-Zamān, for she was like him in figure and in face.
sentences.n: akhfā, Form IV, “to hide, conceal”. lam yashukka aḥadun annahā, “no one doubted that she was”: shakka takes the clause with anna directly, and the sense is that all took her for him. li-annahā, “because she”: li- is “for, because of”, fused with anna. ashbaha, Form IV, “to resemble”. qawām, “stature, figure”.

sentences.t: وَمَازَالَتْ مُسَافِرَةً هِيَ وَأَتْبَاعُهَا أَيَّامًا وَلَيَالِيَ حَتَّى أَشْرَفَتْ عَلَى مَدِينَةٍ مُطِلَّةٍ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ الْمَالِحِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zālat musāfiratan hiya wa-atbāʿuhā ayyāman wa-layāliya ḥattā ashrafat ʿalā madīnatin muṭillatin ʿalā al-baḥri al-māliḥi
sentences.l: And-not she-ceased travelling, she and-her-followers, days and-nights, until she-overlooked upon a-city overlooking upon the-sea the-salt.
sentences.i: She and her following journeyed on, days and nights, until she came in sight of a city that looked out over the salt sea.
sentences.n: The print has ومازات, a misprint for ومازالت, corrected here: wa-mā zālat, “and she did not cease”, which the print sets as one word, kept as set. musāfiratan is accusative as the predicate of zālat. hiya wa-atbāʿuhā, “she and her followers”: the pronoun is repeated so that a second subject can be added. ayyāman wa-layāliya, “days and nights”, accusatives of time; layālī is diptote. ashrafa ʿalā, Form IV, “to come within sight of”, as from a height; aṭalla ʿalā, Form IV, “to overlook”, of a place standing above another. al-baḥr al-māliḥ, “the salt sea”, the sea as against a river: in Classical the adjective is milḥ, and māliḥ is the later form.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَتْ بِظَاهِرِهَا وَضَرَبَتْ خِيَامَهَا فِي ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ لِأَجْلِ الِاسْتِرَاحَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-nazalat bi-ẓāhirihā wa-ḍarabat khiyāmahā fī dhālika al-makāni li-ajli al-istirāḥati
sentences.l: And-she-halted at-its-outside, and-struck her-tents in that place, for-the-sake (of) the-resting.
sentences.i: She halted outside the city and pitched her tents on that spot to rest.
sentences.n: nazala, “to dismount, halt, make camp”. bi-ẓāhirihā, “at its outside”: bi- is “at”, and ẓāhir al-madīna is the open ground outside the walls. ḍaraba khiyāmahu, “to pitch one's tents”. li-ajli, “for the sake of, in order to”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَأَلَتْ عَنْ هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ فَقِيلَ لَهَا هٰذِهِ مَدِينَةُ الْآبَنُوسِ وَمَلِكُهَا الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ وَلَهُ بِنْتٌ اسْمُهَا حَيٰوةُ النُّفُوسِ
sentences.tr: thumma saʾalat ʿan hādhihi al-madīnati fa-qīla lahā hādhihi madīnatu al-ābanūsi wa-malikuhā al-maliku Armānūsu wa-lahu bintun ismuhā Ḥayātu al-Nufūsi
sentences.l: Then she-asked about this city, and-it-was-said to-her: This (is the) City (of) the-Ebony, and-its-king (is) King Armānūs, and-to-him (is) a-daughter, her-name (is) Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.i: Then she asked about the city, and was told, “This is the City of Ebony; its king is King Armānūs, and he has a daughter named Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.”
sentences.n: qīla, “it was said”, the passive of qāla. wa-lahu bintun, “and to him is a daughter”, the Arabic way of saying “he has”. Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, “Life of Souls”: the print spells ḥayāt the old way, حيٰوة, with a dagger alif standing for the long ā; it is kept. Armānūs is a Greek name, and the ebony of the city's name chimes with the Ebony Islands the gardener spoke of. The hamza of سألت and the آ of الآبنوس are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد; they are kept as set.
